analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable standards for immigrant detention and phases out for-profit detention facilities.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on January 27, 2026 with 11 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where no action has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set binding minimum standards for every facility holding immigrants in the custody of the Department of Homeland Security, based on American Bar Association standards. It would require unannounced annual inspections by the department's independent inspector general, public reports on deaths in custody, fines for failing facilities, and termination of contracts with facilities that repeatedly fail. It would end mandatory detention, create a presumption of release with individualized hearings before an immigration judge, prohibit solitary confinement and the detention of children under 18 in ICE facilities, and phase out all contracts with for-profit detention companies and for-profit electronic-monitoring programs within three years. It would also ban fees charged to detainees for monitoring programs and allow detainees to sue facilities that injure them.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants in DHS custody and their families gain enforceable rights: safe conditions, access to counsel and legal orientation, an end to solitary confinement and to detention of children, and the right to sue when they are harmed. Taxpayers gain transparency through public inspection reports, monthly facility data, and contracts open to public records requests. Community-based nonprofits gain contracts to run case management and legal programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Immigrants in detention and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires DHS detention standards at least as protective as the American Bar Association's Civil Immigration Detention Standards, updated at least every two years, with unannounced annual inspector general inspections whose reports must be posted publicly.

Ends mandatory detention: an arrested immigrant must get a hearing before an immigration judge within 48 to 72 hours, with a presumption of release that the government can only overcome with clear and convincing evidence, and bonds set at an amount the detainee can actually pay.
Prohibits solitary confinement for anyone in DHS custody, prohibits detaining anyone under 18 in an ICE facility, and bars DHS from detaining someone solely because they cannot pay a bond.

Phases out all DHS contracts with for-profit detention facility operators and for-profit alternatives-to-detention programs within three years, after which facilities must be owned and operated by the government or nonprofits, and bans charging detainees fees for monitoring programs.

Requires investigation and public reporting of every death in custody within set deadlines, a monthly public online matrix of every detention facility's population and conditions, and updated online detainee location information within 12 hours.

Allows a detained person injured by a standards violation to sue in federal court for damages, injunctive relief, and attorney fees, and guarantees members of Congress unannounced access to inspect any facility.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit detention companies (the government contractors that run most immigrant detention beds) and their shareholders lose their largest customer base when the bill ends for-profit contracts. Taxpayers face short-term transition costs as DHS takes facilities in-house or shifts to nonprofits. Immigration enforcement agencies would lose the presumption-based detention tool and the use of ankle monitors as an alternative to detention.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit detention contractors and, briefly, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Replacing mandatory detention with a presumption of release and a clear-and-convincing standard to detain would let far more people out of custody pending immigration court, a change opponents argue could reduce court appearance rates and complicate enforcement; the government could no longer cite an arrest record alone as grounds to keep someone detained.

Ending ankle-monitor surveillance as an alternative to detention while also ending for-profit contracts would leave the government with fewer monitoring tools, and shifting to government-owned facilities within three years could raise short-term fiscal costs because building and operating facilities directly is expensive up front.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's protections are broad and concrete: enforceable facility standards, due process hearings, an end to child detention and solitary confinement, and public accountability for deaths in custody. The costs are real but mostly transitional: the private detention industry loses a multi-billion-dollar revenue stream, taxpayers may pay more up front to run facilities directly, and enforcement agencies lose some detention and monitoring tools, which supporters consider the point and opponents consider a safety risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and nothing has happened since, so it is waiting on a committee that has shown no sign of taking it up.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill in the Senate on January 27, 2026, along with ten original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, and the action history lists no further steps, hearings, or votes.
The bill has 11 cosponsors in addition to the sponsor — 10 Democrats and 1 independent — and no Senate Republican cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo: for-profit detention contractors keep their contracts, and detainees have no new federal protections. The bill has not been voted on, so no one has won it through the process.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Warren, Welch, Markey, Sanders, Murray, Padilla, Kim, Wyden, Duckworth, and Schiff
for.party: D (Welch is independent, caucusing with Democrats)

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee majority (Chair Chuck Grassley)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over immigration law, chaired by a Republican in the 119th Congress
against.what_they_did: The committee has taken no action on the bill since its January 2026 referral — no hearing, markup, or vote is listed in the action history.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 supporters are Democrats or an allied independent; no Republican senator has cosponsored, and the bill sits in a Republican-chaired committee with no scheduled action.

industries.note: Most immigrant detention beds are run under contract by private companies, including CoreCivic and GEO Group. The bill bars any new such contracts, terminates existing ones within three years, and requires that all detention facilities be government-owned and operated, removing a multi-billion-dollar federal revenue stream. These companies profit per person held in custody, which is why their interest runs against people seeking release.

The bill bars for-profit contracts to run alternatives-to-detention programs and specifically prohibits ankle monitors and other electronic surveillance in the program, cutting off revenue for GPS monitoring of immigrants.

industries.industry: Community-based nonprofits and legal services organizations
industries.note: The bill directs DHS to give contract priority to community-based organizations with experience serving immigrants and refugees, to run a case management program outside ICE, and to operate the Legal Orientation Program at every facility. It also bans charging detainees fees for these services.

analysis.trajectory: Bills to restrict private immigrant detention and end mandatory detention have historically stalled in committee in both chambers, and this one sits in a Republican-chaired committee with no cosponsors from the majority party and no scheduled action. Unless something changes, the most likely path is that it receives no committee vote and expires at the end of this Congress.
